utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. To you too, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. For the record, all the accused are here, also all the Defence teams are present. Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Vanderpuye for the Prosecution. I understand there is a preliminary matter that you would like to raise, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President. Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Judges, good morning, colleagues. Mr. President, I'd like to raise an issue concerning the witness we are about to hear, considering that he is in a special position when compared with other witnesses who have appeared before the Trial Chamber to this day. The witness requested to know from the Prosecution over the weekend, as he was being proofed, whether he was still a suspect, and he was informed that, indeed, he is still a suspect. We believe, Mr. President, that the witness doesn't fully understand what it means to be a suspect, and I'd like to go quickly to the background as to why we say it would be required this morning that the witness be, one, informed by the Prosecution he is a suspect of what, and two, explained by the Trial Chamber what it means to be a suspect. When he testified in the Blagojevic case, he was asked the following question by the Defence because he appeared as a Defence witness at that time: "Have you ever officially been informed that you were no longer a suspect?" Answer was no. That was at page 1981, or 11981, sorry. It's 11981. The witness continued by saying, "I received a summons, I don't know exactly how it all goes. I was called for an interview as a suspect." Same page 11981. At one point the Judge, the Presiding Judge, intervened and stated if the witness still has a status of suspect he is entitled to have a lawyer present in these proceedings. In this case, over the weekend, as I've mentioned he inquired whether he was still a suspect and indeed according to the notes we have received from the Prosecution he is a suspect. During the interview which took place with the Prosecution, the first interview which took place on the 24th of June 2002, throughout the interview, it is our understanding that the witness did not quite understand what it meant to be a suspect. On two occasions he was told the following by the Prosecution. Prosecution, meaning two investigators that he met at that time. I quote from page 87002 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object at this time. We are going into argument about what a witness would have said about potentially the facts, potentially his credibility. This has been done every time we have a witness; there is some sort of argument about the witness. I don't see what we are getting into here right before the witness testifies about an interview and what he said regarding the interview. Many, many of the witnesses we call are suspects. That given the fact that we are not indicting anybody any more is merely a legal designation. Before Mr. Bourgon gets into the facts and details of an interview, I don't really understand at this point how he -- what foundation he has made to get into this. This is a situation where what was said at prior interviews is something that is normally brought up in cross-examination. I don't understand why he's getting into this now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey, for your intervention. Mr. Bourgon, would you kindly finish your submissions and come to the point exactly what your request is?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Do I indeed believe that my colleague's intervention, he should have waited until what I had to say before he stands up. I'm not going to go into the facts of what the witness said. I'm simply going to say that what he was mentioned by the investigators at the time. Now, I say again this was on the June of 2002. He, the witness, was inquiring as to the status of suspect and he was told the following: "The reason you were summoned as witness was because you had information that you were present in Orahovac on the day people were executed." That's page 87002. On page 87003, he was told, "We know you were at the scene of the crime. Until we've talked to you for your explanation, we have to assess; you were seen at the crime, did you participate? This is why you were summoned as a suspect." Page 87003. The idea, Mr. President, is that this witness was met, as I've mentioned earlier, for a full interview of some 100 pages with the Prosecution. Two years later, he appeared as a witness under oath in the Blagojevic case and he testified for quite a bit of time where he was

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, what we'd like to know is now that he has provided the information, now that he has given his story, he's being told that he is still a suspect. If I was this man's lawyer, beyond any doubt he would not be here this morning and I would tell him you have a right not to appear unless you receive a subpoena because you are a suspect. This is dangerous for you. Don't do that. This would be my advice if I was his counsel. Now, the question is: What is he a suspect of? Is it what he said during those interviews that makes him a suspect? Is it what he said that the Prosecution considers not to be true? Or is it something else that he's a suspect unrelated to these events? We believe, Mr. President, that the witness you're about to hear has a right to be informed of what is he a suspect of. Being a suspect contrary to the opinion of my colleague is not just merely a legal thing because we don't indict any more -- we don't indict anyone anymore. We all know in this courtroom that people are being indicted in Sarajevo. I've said that before. All the witnesses who come from the Zvornik are really scared that they might end up in Sarajevo and it would be the least for the Prosecution to tell them what are they a suspect of. This cannot be a way to intimidate. This cannot be used as a way to say, "Listen, always remember you're a suspect. We'll see after your testimony." Now, I'm not saying this happened but that's the way it would appear based on the facts that we know. He also has a right to have a counsel present in this courtroom, as Judge Liu, Presiding Judge in the Blagojevic said. So I sum up, Mr. President, simply by saying I have a double request, a two-pronged request. First, this witness should be informed of what is he a suspect of by the Prosecution, and number two, I would respectfully ask the Trial Chamber to explain to the witness what it means to be a suspect and to testifying as a suspect and that he has a right to get up and leave this courtroom unless of course the Trial Chamber decides to issue a subpoena. But he has a right to get up and leave. That should be made clear to him because these things are never made clear by the Prosecution. He testified once, this witness, and I will simply say that when he did testify he was called as a Defence and at that time he said, "I know that -- I accept to be here because I know I will tell the truth." Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Who is going to respond to that? Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. It's our view this witness is in no different position than many of the other witnesses that have been called by the Prosecution that were present at a crime scene such as Orahovac and we have been dealing with that issue by alerting the Chambers that the witness should be issued a caution which is based on the rules, and that's what we feel is appropriate for this case as well. This person has been explained in response to his question that under the law he is a suspect, as was noted to him. We showed him the law and as you know what the law is, it says basically a person concerning whom the Prosecutor possesses reliable information which tends to show that a person may have committed a crime. This is an extremely broad definition and when you have a soldier that was assigned to go to Orahovac and was tasked to take part in something then it's only fair to let them know that status of a suspect is there to protect them and that's what the caution is based on. And I think we've treated the witnesses appropriately in this case. This witness has been treated appropriately. And I don't see any reason to go away from our standard practice of issuing a caution to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Bourgon? Let's bring this --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Shortly, Mr. President, I disagree with what my colleague is saying that this witness is in the same position as other witnesses. This witness has been -- he inquired himself whether he was still a suspect. He was told he is a suspect. Now, I used the exact word that my colleague just used and I refer to page 6 where it says or the end of page 5 and beginning of page 6, "As you know, the law it says basically a person concerning whom the Prosecutor possesses reliable information which tends to show that a person may have committed a crime." In this case, we have a man who testified in 2004. Now that's three years ago or some three years ago and I don't recall that he has been charged with anything, any charge of perjury. So if he -- if the Prosecution does not believe that the witness lied in 2004, what is the reliable information that they have that he may have committed a crime? I believe, Mr. President, that the Prosecution is simply using the status of suspect because there is the court in Sarajevo, in order to elicit and to get testimony from witnesses. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Bourgon. We need to confer. Sorry, yes, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, just briefly before you begin deliberations I would like you to know that we absolutely join Mr. Bourgon's argument in this instance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you both for your contribution, Mr. Bourgon and Mr. McCloskey, and you, of course, too, Mr. Meek. We'll deal with the witness in the way we think fit in line with what is provided in our rules, as soon as he is sworn in. So let's bring the witness in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On behalf of my colleagues in the Trial Chamber I wish to welcome you to this Tribunal. You're about to start giving evidence. Before you do so, our rules require that you make a solemn declaration equivalent to an oath that you will be testifying the truth throughout the entire -- your entire testimony. And the text -- I see that you already have. Please read out that aloud and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Please make yourself comfortable. You can take a seat and I'll try to explain a few things. Mr. Tanic, I know we are aware that you have already given testimony in another trial as a Defence witness and that this time you have been summoned to give evidence as a witness of the Prosecution, for the Prosecution. We have been told that during your proofing, there was some kind of an exchange between you and the officer who was prosecuting you, with a view to establishing what is your status apart from that of a witness. I'm referring in particular to the question as to whether you are still considered as a suspect by the Prosecution. The reason is that according to what we are told, at some point in time, sometime ago, you were told that you were considered as a suspect. Am I correct so far? Would you agree with me that there was this discussion between you and the interviewer from the Office of the Prosecutor as to your status?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I asked not to be a suspect for four years, either to be put on trial or either not to be a suspect. I do not consider myself to be guilty. I have problems at work. I work in a school and I have this status of a suspect. Somebody might be prone to throw me out of my job, and I have financial problems and all kinds of other problems linked to my status. And this has been going on for four years. So I asked them to lift this, to release me from this, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have you been told why you are a suspect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because on the day of the 14th of July I was with a rifle in Orahovac. That is the only reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have not been given any other reasons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What do you understand your status as a suspect to mean? When someone tells us from the Office of the Prosecutor you still have the status of a suspect, what do you understand from it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As if I have some sort of guilt, as if I was guilty. There are lists being published with the information and people treat you as a participant in the events and you're guilty for it. Simply, it's as if I was really guilt for the event that took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I'll explain to you the definition of a suspect according to our rules, under our rules, so that you will keep it clear in your mind. A suspect, according to our rules, is a person concerning whom the Prosecutor possesses reliable information which tends to show that the person may have committed a crime over which the Tribunal has jurisdiction. So my question to you is the following: Over these last four years, over these last four years, the Prosecution has maintained its position of considering you a suspect and you have maintained your position that you could never be one. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know why I would be a suspect. I'm not saying I was not in Orahovac then but I cannot accept responsibility for what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, I've only got very little more to say to you before you start giving evidence. We as a Tribunal respect an established right, recognised worldwide, given to persons testifying, not to incriminate themselves. Any person has a right not to be forced to incriminate himself, but in this Tribunal, this right is not absolute, so I'm going to explain to you how it goes and then we'll explain to you further what your rights are. In the course of your testimony, questions might be put to you, I'm not saying that they definitely will be put to you, but questions might be put to you from any side, it could be the Prosecution as well as the Defence, which, if answered truthfully, might tend to incriminate you. I'm not saying that this will be the case. But if you are asked questions which, if you answer, would tend to incriminate you, then you have a right to ask us not to answer those questions. In such a case, we have got two options. We can grant your request and exempt you from answering such questions, so that your right against self-incrimination would be protected, or we can compel you, force you, to answer those questions. If we force you to answer those questions, however, you have an additional right. Any answer which you may give, if you are compelled to give that answer, shall not be used as evidence against you in any subsequent prosecution against you for any offence except of course if the offence is of false testimony. I don't know if this right has been explained to you before. If it hasn't, have I explained it well to you and have you understood it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we now proceed with your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I don't know if you want to hear my argument in front of the witness or not but I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the argument is finished. We have decided the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, what the Trial Chamber just put to the witness is not --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object to any further discussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The matter is closed, Mr. Bourgon, please. Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye will be examining you, putting some questions to you. He will then be followed by the various members of the Defence teams on cross-examination. Yes, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I simply have a question for the Trial Chamber and I would like simply to have clarification whether the witness will be informed that he has a right to have a lawyer present and whether he has a right that this testimony is voluntary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is no such right, Mr. Bourgon, please. This only exists in your mind. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, it exists in other trials.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we are going to have a discussion, can we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is no such vested right. Let's put it like this. I mean, unless we hear from the witness that he wants a lawyer present while he is giving testimony, we are not going to go in that direction. Mr. Tanic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it your wish that you have a lawyer present while you give your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Let's proceed. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, good morning to you. Good morning, Your Honours, good morning, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Tanic. I know we are off to a bit of a stressful start but let me just ask you, let me just tell you a couple of things. I'll ask you some questions, as you know. I'm just going to ask you to speak a little bit slowly, slower than you normally would, allow a short pause between the question and answer so that the interpreters can keep up and translate for all the respective parties, and I just also want to remind you that if you feel uncomfortable with respect to certain information that you may be asked about, and you feel a need to answer those questions in private session, I will, of course put that to the Chamber and we can consider whether or not that's possible. Initially I'd like you to start with some background information. Can you tell us first of all how old are you?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: I was born in 1955, so I'm 52.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And where were you born and raised?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: I was born in the village of Tabanci, Zvornik municipality. I went to primary school in Kozluk, I went to secondary school in Zvornik and then I went to the school of economics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you get his name as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you give us your name, and if you could, spell your last name also.

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: My name is Tanacko Tanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you were just saying that you had -- you went to school -- to the school of economics; is that right? Where was that?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Yes. In Novi Sad and I graduated in 1978.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Are you presently employed?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: I work in the high school in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In what capacity? As a teacher?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Teacher, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And how long have you been employed in that capacity?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Four years.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And are you married?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And how long have you been married?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: 25 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, did you complete service with the former JNA?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did my military service in 1981. That's when I finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And between then and 1992, did you hold any employment?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: In that period, I worked in several enterprises, and in 1992, I worked in TG Birac.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Could you just tell us briefly what your responsibilities and duties were in that employment?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Well, my last job was as a planner and analyst in production, making annual estimates of output, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what kind of work did that production involve?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Production of a prefab input for the production of aluminium, semi-manufacturers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, in 1992, were you at some point during that year mobilised?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: The second half of April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And was that to a TO or was that to the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: At that time, it was the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did your unit at some point become a detachment of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Sometime in April. That's when it was established as the Zvornik Battalion or detachment. I don't know what it was exactly according to establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And until when did you serve in the VRS? When were you demobilised?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: I was demobilised sometime in July 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And during that period of time, did you participate in any combat operations or combat, as it were?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court why not?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Well, because in 1992, before that battalion or detachment was established, I had declared that I was not prepared to carry a weapon, so they gave me an easier job. For six months I worked in a logistics platoon cleaning premises, until perhaps the end of October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And at the end of October of 1992, did you receive a different assignment?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Then I moved to the financial section of that battalion or detachment, so I transferred to the financial department within the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you know how it is that you came to be assigned to this financial department or this section? Why you specifically were chosen to do that job?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: I had worked in Standard company for a long time on such jobs and then when a predecessor took sick leave I was invited to take over and that's where I stayed until the end. And they knew in fact that I had a degree in economics and that I had experience in such things, and that I was able.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could you describe for the Trial Chamber what specific tasks or duties you had in the financial department?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Payments for whatever was needed for logistics and payments of wages to soldiers. Payments in and out for the requirements of the logistics, and paying out the wages of soldiers, unit by unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And when you say paying out the wages of soldiers, do you mean by actually distributing cash, as it were?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Yes. Certain amounts were paid out according to lists, to every soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in terms of payments for items related to logistics, could you just tell us what those types of items are?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Well, some basic needs. What do I know? We would write our requirements and then we would collect from the treasury, when some purchases needed to be made, they would go to the treasury, get the money, for all sorts of needs. I don't remember anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the relevance of this? Why are you prolonging your list of questions on this issue, on this matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I was actually just about to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Who were you responsible to in this capacity?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. It was assistant commander for logistics in the brigade, and if it concerned operations, the assistant commander for logistics could issue orders to me directly and the commander could supervise our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you in this capacity have occasion to meet with the brigade commander on a regular basis?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: It was not on a regular basis. At some stage, I was chief of finances briefly and later I was the treasurer. The chief of finance goes to report to the commander more often, and would see him more often. But in my position I would not see him on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now in July 1995, could you tell us what your position was?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Treasurer at the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And could you tell us were you assigned to the barracks?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And could you describe for the Trial Chamber where your office was in the barracks?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Well, in 1995, it was on the ground floor of the barracks. I don't know exactly how to describe it. On the ground floor of that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just direct your attention to the 14th of July 1995. Do you remember that day?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: I remember some details, of course, but since lots of things happened during those days, I don't remember everything. I remember some things about the 14th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I guess the first thing I'll ask you is do you remember if you were working on that day, in the morning?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Business as usual. I was within the compound of the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did anything unusual occur that morning? Did you see or hear anything unusual that morning?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't remember everything now. I know the activities around Srebrenica had begun earlier and they were ongoing. They were continuous from the beginning of the operation until the end of the operation. Everything was related to Srebrenica. I don't know what I could add. Nothing changed as far as my work concerned. There were events but I can neither relate them nor remember them now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Can you tell us, as best as you remember, what you did that morning? Up until, say, around noon.

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: The usual. I was at my office. I don't remember if there was an inspection of troops even. The standard usual activities. I didn't notice that there was an increased number or concentration of troops. I have already related all that I saw in previous statements and interviews. I can't remember in detail now. I was doing my usual work. I would go into adjacent offices or I would go upstairs to the cafeteria for lunch.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Well, did there come a certain point during that day when you left the Standard?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Yes. I went to Orahovac. And before departing for Orahovac, I didn't leave the compound at all. Maybe I went as far as the gate, and I went to Orahovac because Mijatovic came along and said that the prisoners were escaping. I don't remember if he mentioned at what location but he told me to get my rifle and go. And he said that in passing, in a rush. I took my rifle then and left. And a small truck was already standing there at the Standard waiting. I got into that vehicle and left.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You mentioned Mijatovic. Just so we are clear for the record, could you tell us who that is?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: He was in the commercial purchases section of the brigade. He had been wounded. He had undergone surgeries. I don't know. After that, he was transferred to the commercial section.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, did he have a rank?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe in the reserve force he had a rank of captain but what exactly that means, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, you've said that he asked you to get your rifle. Is that an order?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: I don't know. He was in a rush. He said the prisoners were running away and he told me to get out and go. I don't know exactly to what location. I cannot remember it all in sequence now but I had already heard probably that there were some prisoners somewhere, and he said that the prisoners were running away and I thought I would go there and help out so that they wouldn't all disperse and I didn't know if those prisoners -- if those people were thirsty or hungry so I thought I would go out and help.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, you said that you had heard probably that there were some prisoners somewhere. Could you just tell us what it is that you heard?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Well, I suppose I had known already that there were already prisoners detained before I heard that they were escaping. So as soon as I was told they were escaping, I knew what it was about. I knew that there were some prisoners somewhere. And I had heard at that time that they were located, detained in some schoolhouses but I don't recall. On the 14th, in the morning, there was a bus outside the gates. I wasn't paying much attention but I heard later that that bus wandered around some places finding nowhere to put those people up. I heard that from somebody but how exactly it was related to me, in what words, I can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, if you could ask the witness in what capacity Mijatovic told the witness to go to Orahovac. For example, if he was a duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I'll put that to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Have you understood His Honour's question, Mr. Tanic? Okay.

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: No. He was not the duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you have a recollection of what his position was?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: I've already said that. I don't know to which unit he belonged formally but he worked in the purchases department of the logistics. I don't remember paying out his wages. I can't remember clearly now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't take it, Mr. Tanic, that Mr. Mijatovic is your superior because you were working at financial department, and he was in the commercial section. So why did he tell you to go to Orahovac, in what capacity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know. Maybe quite simply he received orders from somebody. He came in, saw me standing there in the hallway, and if I hadn't been there in the hallway I may not have been summoned at all. But as he was passing by, he told me, "Get your rifle and come." What did I know? I didn't know what was going on and why. I understood it was an emergency. I understood something was going on. That's why I did get my rifle and left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge Kwon's question is a very relevant one. Was Mr. Mijatovic in a position to give you orders? Did you consider him at the time to be a person in a position to give you orders which you had to obey?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not that I believed that. It's that I believed what he said, that they were escaping, and it had more to do with the fact that we were in good terms and he was on good terms with the commander of the brigade, and I thought maybe somewhere along the line I might have problems if I disobey. At any rate, I decided it's better to do as he says than to decline.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When you say that he was on good terms with the commander of the brigade, could you just explain what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Well, all the purchases and whatever was needed for the brigade was obtained. There were no problems. It was approved, and allowed, and that is why I thought that they collaborated well. There were no problems. And he would say the commander said or the assistant commander for logistics told me to give him so much money. That is what I would do. So I don't know how to explain it. He was an authority, all of them were for me of authority, especially in wartime.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you feel that he was in a position with the commander that could cause you problems if you didn't follow what he told you to do?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's answered the question in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We do not interrupt my colleague but this is -- there are limits to leading questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Your objection is fully sustained, Mr. Bourgon. Please move to your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You had mentioned something about having heard that this bus that you saw went to various -- or to some schools. Can you tell us what it is that you heard in relation to those schools?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: I don't know the details. It was a long time ago. I just know that one of those buses was there. I can't remember whether there were more than one but one of them had problems. They couldn't find a location to put them up in. That was the story that reached me so it wandered left and right from one locality to another. Where it ended up and where those people were put up in the end, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Just so the record is clear, you haven't mentioned anything about people so far. Were there people on the buses? Or on the bus?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: It wasn't empty, of course, there were people in one of them. Of course, there were people there, and they spent the night there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What people were they?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Prisoners probably. I don't know. I didn't go up to them. I wasn't specially interested. I didn't really like to inquire. I didn't ask where they had come from because there was nothing I could do for them. I just didn't know. I didn't show an interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: At the time that you were asked to grab your rifle and go, could you tell us what you did next?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: I simply picked up my rifle, went out to the compound, outside the barracks, and there was a small truck which had come from somewhere, whether it was a shift or something, I boarded this vehicle and went off to Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Were there other people on the truck?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: There were, but I really can't remember exactly who they were. One makes mistakes all one's life but I could have gone back but I was ashamed of those in the truck for me to go back. Since they were going, I felt I should go too. Because after that, nobody said anything to me. I could have gone back but when they had seen me, once they saw me in the compound, I felt embarrassed to go back so I boarded the truck and joined them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And could you just tell us about how many people were on the truck?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: I don't know. It was a small vehicle. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What happened next?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Nothing. I got off the vehicle, we got out of the vehicle. I think we were taken to the road. I can't remember exactly. We got off there, near the fence of the gym. In the yard there were some troops there already. I don't know what else I could say.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Around what time did this occur?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I think it was after 12.00 but I can't be quite sure about the time. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When you got off the truck, this is at -- this is at the school in Orahovac, right?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When you got off the truck, what did you see?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: In the playground, there were some people, there were some soldiers. There were some people on the road too and also within the schoolyard. I don't know what else.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When you say there were people there and soldiers, are you distinguishing between civilians and soldiers or could you just tell us who these people were?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Soldiers, soldiers. There were troops, mostly there were no civilians. It was just troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And where did you see the troops initially?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Mostly, most of them were in the yard, in front of the gym. I don't know exactly how many they were but there were some.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And could you tell from looking at these troops what units they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: At the time, I could know but now I can't tell you exactly who they were, which unit they belonged to. There were some military policemen and the rest were soldiers. Earlier on, I would be able to tell you, but I can't remember any longer who they were, who the troops -- which unit the troops belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When you say soldiers, can you tell us what brigade these soldiers belonged to?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: The Zvornik Brigade, I assume. I don't know of any others there. And I know that I saw a policeman in uniform. I was close, and he said that he had come from Doboj, that he belonged to the Doboj police. That was just one person that I actually saw. I didn't really look closely. When I saw what was happening and what was expected, I have this picture as if I was looking through the binoculars and you turn them upside down. It's as if I was looking from a distance because I was revolted by the event. I saw that they were not escaping, and I don't know what was going on. I didn't see anything special. And what was typical, what I remember, was the noise of the people as if they were in a beehive. Now, whether it was talking, so from the road, I could hear this -- this noise, this humming, but the picture I had was as if I had turned the binoculars upside down and was looking, it all seemed so unreal and distant. And that was the impression I had. It was unpleasant.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you actually see any prisoners after you arrived?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: When I entered, as I was there, my movements were mostly, I went inside there once or twice, and when I did, closer to the fence, there were two dead bodies. Now, whether they were wearing coats or were covered by their coats, I don't know but somebody pointed them out to me. Otherwise I wouldn't notice. He nudged me as we were standing there and showed me those two dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And where did you see these two dead bodies?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Right in the yard, closer to the fence, closer to the road, in one of the corners. That was the picture in my mind. Now, the exact spot, but I did see them. I think it was there, where I said. And in front of the main entrance to the gym, I saw a pile of clothing, and I think there was a crutch there too in the pile of clothes. And this whole event is -- that is what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You indicated that -- you referred to a humming, a noise. Could you describe what it is that you heard? Did you hear humming in terms of a noise or did you hear talking or anything of that nature? If you could just elaborate for us what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. Maybe several people were talking at the same time but from the outside, it sounded like a buzzing, a humming, as if I was one metre away from a beehive.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you spend any time with anybody that you knew while you were at the school?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: When I saw what the situation was, I myself, conditionally speaking, took upon myself the obligation together with Cedo Jovic and Goran Bogdanovic who were members of the military police, I stood on the road so that civilians and women shouldn't approach the yard because the road passes there and I stood there with them for a while. I moved along the gym and the school to the cultural centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In the yard at the school, did you see any officers that you recognised?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: In the yard, I saw, before me, I don't know how they got there, there was Sreten Milosevic, Drago Nikolic. I don't know who else.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you see any officers that you did not recognise?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: At one point in time, I was standing on the road, I saw in the yard people who were unknown to me. Then I asked one of the military policemen, I don't know his name, and I asked him who is that one? And he said a security officer from the corps, Vujadin Popovic. But I don't know the man at all. It is just what he told me. They told me that that was who it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you recall what the person that you saw looked like at that time?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: No, no. I can't. Not now. I know he had some rank. I can't even remember or describe him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: With respect to Sreten Milosevic, can you tell us what his position was?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: He was assistant commander for logistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us what it is you saw him doing?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't say anything what people were doing within that schoolyard, around the main gate. I really cannot confirm whether they were preparing to organise taking those people out of the gym. I can't say what they -- exactly they were doing, what duties they had. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: With respect to Drago Nikolic, can you tell us what his position was then and what he was doing?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: He was chief of security in the brigade. What exactly he was doing and how he was working, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us where it is you saw him?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Within the same yard there, in front of the gym. That's where they were. I didn't spend a lot of time there. I saw that I wasn't important for anyone, no one was asking me anything in particular, and I sort of simply, on my own initiative, went along the road, and for a time I saw some young boys carrying water. That added to my nervousness. I thought to myself, why don't they separate the children? The reaction was that they would grow up and then one of the reasons why I didn't take part in that because there were children of the same age as my own there, and that was another reason, conditionally speaking, for me to be extremely, I don't know how to put it, I felt so upset that I didn't know what to do. You see what's going on, but what can you do? I can pick up a rifle and kill two or three of, shall I call them ours? And then someone will kill me and what was planned would be carried out nevertheless. And now, as I look at the event from this distance, it's better that I didn't. I couldn't have killed anyone. If I had tried to do anything, it would have had a negative effect on me. I couldn't have achieved anything. Nobody would look after my children. I would have hurt myself without achieving anything so I was revolted and impotent and there was nothing I could do and I was very angry about it all but really I could not do anything. But I must say no one asked me to do anything. I simply was not in a position to do anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You mentioned these children. Can you tell us about how old you thought that you believed they were?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: I don't know, about ten. At one point, I went to the cultural centre, up the steps, and Mihajlo Stevanovic was there and Milan Savic, they were there. And then I saw a boy carrying a bucket of water, along the back side of the school towards the gym. I couldn't see the gym or anything but when I passed there, I saw them continuing to carry water. How many children there were, I don't know. Boys, boys, 10 or 12. They were small, young boys.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could you tell us approximately how many there were or how many you saw?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: I know I saw this one carrying water and then when I was passing by the gym, I think I saw two boys in all. Whether there were more of them, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you receive any assignment or task while you were at the school?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I simply could have sort of avoided any position where I was too conspicuous so for a while I sat on the steps that I already mentioned and then across the way there is a house behind the school, we spent some time there. Then I would come back again to see whether anyone was looking for me, whether there were any problems, and then I went to Orahovac to Mira Davidovic's [as interpreted] and I stayed there until 7.00 or 8.00, I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Were you ever asked by anyone to participate in any execution?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's a leading question and the question was posed to the witness whether he was asked anything or he was given any task and the witness answered no and now we are coming back again with another question which is leading in that it is suggesting that he may have been told to shoot somebody. Now, this is -- the question has been asked, it's been answered and it's a leading question. We should ask the witness not say what my colleague is looking for but he should simply ask an open question. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Vanderpuye, your comments on this, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I can rephrase the question if that will satisfy my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Keeping in mind also what the witness said according to the transcript on lines 9 and 10 on page 28, namely: "But I must say no one asked me to do anything. I simply was not in a position to do anything." So if you are going to rephrase your question, go ahead, do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Were you ever issued any orders while you were at the school?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The question has been asked and answered, Mr. President. I refer to page 29 or page 28 lines 25 and page 29 lines 1 and 2. "Did you receive any assignment or task while you were at the school?" Answer: "No, I didn't. I could have sort of avoided any position where I was too conspicuous" and then he goes on. We should limit ourselves to one time those questions and now he's had two opportunities. I think it's time to move on, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, your comments, your remarks?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think that's actually a distinct question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In what sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The question I asked before was whether he received an assignment or task and that doesn't necessarily entail an order and I think Mr. Bourgon is well aware of that. The witness answered previously I should add in relation to his boarding of the truck, I think he was specifically asked a similar question and the answer that he gave was that it wasn't an order, and I think that that distinguishes the question that I put to the witness at this point from the prior question and answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think in the first place that this debate should continue in the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That's exactly what I was going to say, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You will conclude with this on this issue, Mr. Vanderpuye. We consider that an order is more pointed, more specific, than an assignment or a task or a mere asking. So you can put the question and that will be the last time you are addressing this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you kindly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, while you were at the school, were you given any order?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: When I was at the school, I didn't receive any particular order. If somebody who knew me came close to the fence and said, "Come along, do you want to do some shooting," I can't remember exactly who it was but it wasn't in the form of an order. It was a sort of casual question. And I refused but nothing happened. There were no consequences. I didn't have any consequences as a result of that. Because they knew I wasn't prepared to do such a thing. I can't exactly name who said this to me but somebody who knew me. I don't remember exactly who it was. And I don't think it will be fair to mention someone when I'm not sure. So there was this question when I was close to the fence, somebody said, "Would I?" But not in the form of an order. Just as in the form of a question. I refused it and I didn't take part.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: My colleague is indicating to me that this is just about time for the break. This would probably be a good point to stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will have a 25-minute break starting from now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good morning again, Mr. Tanic. Just before the break, in relation to a question that I had asked you, you had indicated that someone had come along and asked you do you want to do some shooting? What did you take that to mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I think we've completed with this one, Mr. President. My learned friend is glad enough to have been able to ask this question, he got the full answer from the witness exactly what happened, what he remembers. There is no need to go back again into this topic, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you wish to comment on that, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I believe that it is a relevant question and I believe that the witness can elaborate on that answer in order to sufficiently identify what he understood of that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's important for the witness to specify what he understood and why he refused it and didn't take part. So to understand exactly what he was talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But he answered the question, Mr. President, already, in detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, when it's time for you to take my place, or the place of any of us four up here, you will know, but it's not yet arrived. So let's proceed. Could you answer the question, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the person who directed me, I can't remember exactly now who it was and I don't want to speculate. In fact I know who it was that asked me, it's just that I can't remember now, and it wasn't in the form of an order, it was just casual like, would you like to go shoot people? It wasn't in the form of an order. It was put in a way that I could decline and nothing happened. And then there was this other comment. I cannot tell you for sure the identity of the person. It was somebody who knew me and whom I knew well enough to say no, and there were no consequences for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That wasn't the question. Probably the reason for you answering a different question is that we allowed [Microphone not activated] interval of time. The question was the following, sir,

utterances.speaker: MR. TANIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye asked you, told you the following: "Just before the break in relation to a question that I had asked you you had indicated someone had come along and asked you do you want to do some shooting?" The question is the following: When this person approached you, what did you take his words or his invitation to mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That I don't have to participate in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Participate in what?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand that I was obliged to take part in the execution because it was an invitation that they would give me a different kind of weapon. They asked me whether I would like to shoot, but I knew the person and I was able to decline and I could say no. In fact, it's out of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: At the time that this person came to you and asked you those questions, was that during the time that Drago Nikolic was still at the school?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot define it precisely now. I knew that at some point certain people were there, but after that, who was where, I don't know. I don't know whether he was there at that time. At the time of the other scene that I described, I was standing by the road and the person and persons who invited me were standing in the schoolyard. So it implied that they would have given me a different kind of weapon if I had accepted. I cannot tell you anything about the persons who were moving around the schoolyard. I can only say that I was there for a relatively short time, two or three hours in total, and I tried to describe to you everything I saw, as best I could. As for the details after all these years, I cannot remember every detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You indicated before that you were revolted by the event. Would you tell us what it is --

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: In that period of time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Would you tell us what it is that you found revolting?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Well, because conditionally speaking, it was obvious that there would be some organisation, there was no question of transport, and there were children there as well. These people were detained. I don't know. I did not believe for a moment that it would happen but when it happened, it did. At that time, I could see that there were children there and there was no reason, no cause, but there was no question of an exchange either. And then it became obvious that they would be executed and the children would be executed but what could I do? I couldn't do anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could you tell us when it became obvious to you, when those things became obvious to you?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Well, I was there until the first group started boarding a truck. I didn't wait for them to finish boarding the truck. When the first group started boarding the truck, I could already see. Well, the first group, when they set out. Well, it was obvious that it was not going to be an exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Why do you say it was obvious it was not going to be an exchange and what information did you have about any exchange?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Well, because -- I don't know. There was some talk before that they would go for an exchange. As long as I was standing around, it was-- it seemed to be an option, that they would be exchanged but as soon as they started boarding, I saw that nothing would come of that. So I just tried to make myself scarce from that area, from the schoolhouse, Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Were you told anything specific with respect to the possibility of an exchange?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: No. I don't know. There was a story circulating that some negotiations were going on with them. Those were stories. I didn't hear it firsthand. That there would be maybe an exchange and they would not be -- they would not be placed in vehicles, but then finally they were. That's a story I heard. That's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you hear about who may have been involved in those negotiations?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The witness said it's a story he heard. Do you want to hear what stories he heard or do you want to hear what the witness saw and heard? This is a story he heard about. Do we want to know what the witnesses, the stories they hear? Is that what this trial is about, stories the witness may have heard? I don't think so, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, do you wish to comment on that, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I do acknowledge my colleague's concern for hearsay evidence, it hasn't been elicited from the witness from whom he heard this information. I think whom he hears the information from is important to the reliability of the information, and I understand that it's not entirely excludable merely because it's hearsay but I certainly don't have a vested interest in pursuing this matter and I'll happily move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But we think that the question should be answered because if he heard stories, if he can tell us from whom he heard these stories and if there were people mentioned in the course of these stories, that becomes important to complete his previous answer. Yes, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like if we could begin by who he heard it from, whether it's one person or many persons or rumours or so that we have some kind of a basis before we hear the stories.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you for your suggestion, Mr. Bourgon. So perhaps I can deal with this straight away myself. Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: A short while ago you told us there was a story circulating that some negotiations were going on with them. "Those were stories. I didn't hear it firsthand. That there would be maybe an exchange and that they would not be -- they would not be placed in vehicles. But then finally they were. That's a story I heard." From whom did you hear this story?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. It's been said already. If I was on one side of the fence and they were on the other side of the fence in the schoolyard and that information reached that point where I was standing next to the schoolyard, I cannot tell you the names of the people who passed it on to me. It was just like grapevine. People were talking about what was going on. I don't know what was going on. I don't know what was going on either outside the locker room or closer to that door but there was talk that negotiations would proceed, that they would not be boarding vehicles, they had been promised that they would be exchanged, but later on, they were placed in vehicles and there was no exchange. How am I supposed to give you names now? I can tell you, conditionally speaking, that I heard that, for instance, Drago Nikolic was going to conduct these negotiations but I cannot assert that, I cannot claim that with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Was any other person mentioned in relation to the possible negotiations that you heard might have been going on at the time? Apart from Drago Nikolic that you have just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you left the area of the school?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: I went to Orahovac, to a house that is almost a kilometre away. The house of Mira Vidovic. So from the school, one kilometre in the direction of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us how much time you spent at that house, approximately?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, maybe from 6.00 to perhaps 8.00, a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us generally and briefly what were you doing while you were there?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Well, I sat there with them, discussed that event. I don't know. There was her mother-in-law there, her children. I don't remember if the husband was there but he probably was. We were talking about what was going on. I don't know how I managed to tell her what I told her about what was going on. I knew that woman Mira because she had worked in the treasury before the war. I knew her from that time. So I went to her place to visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When you left the area of the school to go to her house, did you leave there alone or did you leave there were other people?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And when you left her house --

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: I don't know. It was already dark, and I tried to walk to Standard.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Had you made any prior arrangement to get back to Standard before you left the school area?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: No. I had not. I hadn't asked anyone, and when I went there, I didn't intend to stay for such a long time in the first place, but I did, and when I got out, it was already dark. It might have been 10.00 or 10.30, maybe even later.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: After you left, can you tell us what you did?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Well, I took the road, and I was maybe -- maybe 150 to 200 metres from her house. When I stopped because it was kind of awkward, there was shooting that I could hear, some sort of front line was in the vicinity. I didn't know what kind of shooting I was hearing. And I stood there thinking that somebody might come along and something might happen to me, so I stood there and I thought that since I had a rifle on me I should put some munitions in it. I had an M-48 so I rifled through my pockets. I had ammunition in my pockets. I didn't -- I managed to cock the rifle, to pull the safety lock, so I just stood there waiting for somebody I knew to give me a lift.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can we go into private session for a moment, please, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sure. Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We are now in open session so I'm just going to ask you to refrain from mentioning any names. You indicated that the van went in the direction of Zvornik. Did you take any other route?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: No. There is no other route, not that I know of. That's the main road.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you've indicated that it went to the Standard; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Were you -- did everybody in the van go to Standard?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Everybody got out outside the Standard, except the boy. The driver and the boy continued on to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in which direction was that?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: In the direction of Zvornik, further on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And when you say everybody got out outside the Standard, where are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: I got out, Sreten, Mijatovic, Mihajlo and the logistics man and the driver with the boy drove on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I understand that, but where did that occur?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: I don't remember if the vehicle actually got into the compound or left us outside the building near the entrance. I can't remember anymore. We just got out of the van and the van drove on with the boy inside. I cannot tell you the exact location. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What did you do when you got back to the Standard?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: I went to the office, stayed there for a while, put down the rifle. I don't know how long I spent there. And then I thought I would go upstairs and then I saw that the office of the logistics commander was open, Sreten's office, so I stopped by.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And is that upstairs, in fact?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the upper floor. His office was the next one after the duty officer's.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what, if anything, was going on at that office?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Well, when I came, I can't tell you exactly if it was at the same moment but -- could you -- could we go into private session for this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection to that? Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In response to the president's question, you've indicated that (redacted) was referring to what happened in Orahovac. Was he talking about what a good job the prisoners, that the soldiers did, guarding the prisoners? Was that your understanding?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: No. That was not my understanding. But generally, that it had been done the way it had been done and that it was a good job.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Are you referring to the executions?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In terms of what you saw while you were in Orahovac --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry, that was -- I regret having suggested that we go back into open session because this (redacted) and supposedly the words he said was all done or heard in private session. And we can't have the two reconciled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So please redact from line 3 on page 45 -- yes, but I think even the whole context. Let's go into private session for a short while, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think I was just about to ask you, while you were in Orahovac, you indicated that you saw Drago Nikolic. Do you have any doubt in your mind that that's who you saw?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: No, no. The people I mentioned I saw them. When exactly they came, when they left, I don't know those details.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you see Miladin Mijatovic there?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Any doubt about that?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: No, I have none.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you see Sreten Milosevic there?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Any doubt about that?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: No, I have none.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Cedo Jovic, Goran Bogdanovic, did you see them there?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Any doubt about that?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic? Let me just update the list that I have been handed. Mr. Zivanovic requires one hour?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Beara team half an hour?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Perhaps shorter, Mr. President, if at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Nikolic? You required an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'll probably need longer, Mr. President. There is lots of stories this witness heard that I want to get into.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Borovcanin team? None?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No cross for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Miletic? Ten minutes?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no questions for this witness, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Still nothing, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Pandurevic, 30 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That would be accurate currently, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So we start with Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Tanic. I had occasion to read carefully your earlier statement. I first read your interview which you granted to the investigators of the OTP on the 25th of June 2002. In that interview, I saw that you received the invitation to attend from the police, our police.

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, in that invitation or summons, was it -- was there an indication whether you had to respond, whether there would be any sanctions if you failed to attend?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: I don't know who it is that sends these summons but somebody, a worker from the SUP, brought this document with a date indicated and saying that I was a suspect for the events linked to Srebrenica on the 14th of July. So I don't know what else I should say. That I was a suspect. So as soon as I was given this document by the police, with a date indicated, I felt I had to go. And let me just add in a kind of attachment, it said that I would not be arrested within a period of 15 days, these letters were attached to the summons with these explanations. So when I go there and come back, that I would not be arrested. I could come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, you might be arrested five days later?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: From this interview, I gather that the investigators took that summons from you. Was it returned to you or did they keep it?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: I can't remember whether it was copied, whether it was returned. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, were you told that as a suspect, you don't have to answer questions put to you by the investigator?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you why I'm asking you this. You say that you were. I have some different information. In this interview of yours, for the sake of orientation, tape 2, track A, you say, among other things, that you are not obligated to talk about others, and the investigator says, and this is line 12, of course, you are entitled not to answer a certain question. Was your understanding that you could refuse to answer questions generally or that there were one or two questions that you could not answer?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: I asked why I was a suspect and that was my main problem, but on the side of the investigators, they just said that that was the procedure and that I had to, but I know that I was told that I was entitled to a lawyer, et cetera, and that I don't have to answer questions but then I could have not answered any but I don't know how these things work so...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This interview of yours of the 25th of June 2002, was recorded. I would like to ask you, before the taping of your interview started, the recording, did you talk to the investigators?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll tell you why I'm asking you this. Again in this transcript of the interview, I saw that at a certain point in time, when the investigator asked you in which schools the Muslims were held, because they were asking you about some other schools, whether you were aware of that, you say, "We said we wouldn't. I, Orahovac, guilty, not guilty." That was your response, so my conclusion was that you had some sort of conversation before the recording started because I don't find a recording of this statement in the transcript itself.

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
