utterances.text: I don't know. I don't remember. I just know that I always insisted on this status of suspect being removed, that I should be either tried or something. Surely I have some basic human rights, the right to work. Anyone can fire me and after my testimony here, I may not even be entitled to life, the right to life, so it's a very serious problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me now draw your attention to another segment of your interview. Among other things, the investigator asked you a precise question which I will quote and it is tape 4, track A, page 12 out of a total of 16, and line 15 to 18, lines 15 to 18. The investigator asks,"So perhaps Popovic was not in the school." And your answer, "It's best for you to cross him out, cross him out. How do I know now whether he was there or not, who was there, it was ten years ago." I've read out this as something you said. But I believe that your answer was in accord with your recollection. My question is: Is that the same answer you would give today?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Not they. I don't know how an examination is done. If you mention a name, it goes round in a circle, where, how, when, who, what kind of vehicle, which man, where was he, what was he wearing, et cetera. There are a thousand and one details and it was a long time ago and I had had enough of this going back to the same issue and so I apologise to anyone if I harmed them but there it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me just remind you that at the time you mentioned as an act by this officer who you were talking about, I'm sorry, that the rank of this officer was a major.

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Maybe. I asked who he was and that is what they told me. Never mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me now ask you again reading your previous interview and statement because you already testified here before, and today's testimony, I saw a small discrepancy with respect to the bus that you referred to. Earlier, you said this was on the 15th in the morning. Now you said it was on the 14th in the morning.

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Then I must have made a mistake but it was on the 14th in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So you're sure of that?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Then I won't ask you any more about that. You have described in some detail your return from Orahovac that night of the 14th of July, and you described how you got back, with whom. I won't mention any names because there are protected witnesses among them or someone may become a witness and ask for protective measures. I just wanted to tell you, or rather to point out to you, that we have had occasion to hear -- could we please go into private session after all? Private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll have the break now, 25 minutes, and then Mr. Bourgon will start his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Tanic, or good afternoon. How are you today?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I notice that in the meantime, Mr. Meek has left us, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President, he's working out of the office this afternoon, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: He's working elsewhere in the building, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you both. Mr. Bourgon, my apologies for the interruption. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, I'd like to begin by going over with you briefly the number of times you were met by the Prosecution, as well as by the Defence, leading up to your testimony today. First question is: Do you recall that your interview with the office of the Prosecution took place on the 24th of June 2002?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: The 24th or the 25th? It should be right. That should be right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you recall that your testimony in the Blagojevic case, even though you might not know the exact date was on 16th of July 2004?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you recall meeting with me personally on the 10th of June 2006, as well as on 16 March of this year?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: I know we met and talked but I don't remember dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you recall also meeting with the investigator assigned to the team I work with on a couple of occasions?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, my questions today are based on the material that I have that you provided both the office of the Prosecution when you testified under oath as well as when you and I had the occasion to meet and when you met with the investigator assigned to this team. First I'd like to begin by asking you about the proofing session which took place with the Prosecution yesterday or Saturday, I'm not sure. I think it went over the weekend. When did you actually meet with the Prosecution this weekend?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Do I have to answer these questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Indeed you do, Mr. Tanic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think. We tell him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then it was on Saturday, Saturday. I think so. Yes. These past days.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you recall that as you were -- as you met with the Prosecution, you made, you compiled some handwritten notes because these notes were given to us. Do you recall making these notes?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: When? Yesterday? Which notes?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Over the weekend, three pages of notes that you left with the Prosecution while you met with them this weekend.

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: I shouldn't have left it. I was going to take it with me. They are my own intimate notes. I -- surely, those are my notes, not notes of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, because these notes were given to us by the Prosecution, as is the practice, and what I'd like is I have a few questions to ask you on these notes. If you need the notes, if you want to refer to them, I have a copy here. They are not in e-court, Mr. President, because they were -- we just received them last night and they were translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. On the other hand, I think I need to explain to the witness so that he doesn't get carried away that something irregular has taken place. It is the duty, the responsibility, of the Prosecution to pass on all information, to disclose all information, about the exchanges that take place during the proofing session, to the members of the Defence teams. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I just have two quick questions, Mr. Tanic. The first is I refer to one of those pages of your notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's make it available to him, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I only have a paper copy, Mr. President. If we can show it to my colleague to show that the pages correspond. This is the original version in B/C/S. I have a translation with me but we had to do that on our own last night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye, for confirming. Yes, your question, Mr. Bourgon, or questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My first question simply is I look on the page, I'm not sure, there are two pages with a number 1 on top. And one has to do with, as you were listening to the tape. Do you find this page? It says on top, listening to the tape. And there is a one on the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I move to the second bullet point on the top of that page where it says, "I was wrong not to ask for a lawyer." Can you explain why you were wrong or you believe you were wrong not to ask for a lawyer?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Probably in that case I would have fewer problems. Then he might tell me that I don't have to answer questions. That was my understanding. If I had taken a lawyer then on the 24th of June in Banja Luka and here, I probably wouldn't have had to answer certain questions. I don't really know how that procedure works but I could have avoided some unpleasantness that I've created for myself but I thought these were my notes. I didn't make them for the public. I could have put them in my pocket. I don't quite understand. I made these notes listening to the tape to remind myself of things, not for this to be any kind of an original document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to refer you to the page of your notes which has a number 3 at the top. And the first line reads, "Around first lineup."

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Yes. And what?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, on this page, there is a line which actually is underlined where it says, "Now I have problems." So that's basically --

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: That is my note. I can't listen to the tape again. This was my understanding. I don't know. I can't. I wrote this down listening to the tape. So as to remind myself internally. I didn't think this would be used. I don't understand this. Listening to the tape, I jotted these things down. I can't remember what was the context or anything. I really don't know. I made this -- these notes for myself. I didn't know. I could have put it in my pocket and taken them with me. The tape was on and I was making the notes. I don't understand how this now can be used. I don't know. I would need to listen to the tape again to know what it is I wrote down because the tape went on for some two or three hours. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The only reason I asked this question, Mr. Tanic, is simply because we have the notes and I was curious as to those two lines and I will stop there. I move to my next question. As a result of your proofing session with the Prosecution, we were also given a supplemental information sheet, and we were informed by that document, and I will quote the text, "The witness confirmed that he had reviewed the transcript of the interview and listened to his trial testimony." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And it goes on to say, "He was asked if he found any errors and the witness indicated that the statements were correct, save a reference to some stairs." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if I go on, it says, "The witness further indicated that he stands" - well, the word "by" is not there but I believe there should be a word - "he stands his prior testimony and statement." So do you stand by both the testimony and the statement?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: I suppose so. I really don't know what --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, my colleague representing another accused in this case mentioned to you about a discrepancy which he found between the testimony and the interview, and I'd just like to ask you whether you can confirm that if there are details that are not exactly the same from the interview to the testimony, that the interview would be more accurate because it was closer to the events in 2002? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: I don't agree with you because in 2002 I thought the steps belonged to the school, but I didn't go to Orahovac often. I didn't put it properly, that the steps were of the cultural centre, and I didn't pay any attention until I went to see the stairs of the school and then I saw that those stairs were not of the school, then with Mihajlo Stevanovic went with me and showed me the steps where we were which is behind the cultural centre so I told the Prosecution I had a correction. I really thought it was of the school but that was what I thought at the time. And that is why I tried to correct that portion, saying that the steps did not belong to the school but of the cultural centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I thank you for your answer because it is an area we will go into in terms of the stairs at the -- where you stood but for now, I'm just asking a general question because there are some discrepancies between the interview and the testimony. So I take it -- I'm asking you which one would be more accurate, your -- the interview or was it the testimony?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, yes, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I do object. I think he's answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, he answered the question in respect of one detail but he did not answer the question in general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But what do you mean by the question in general? Because --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In general, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your question was limited to the stair factor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The question was not limited to the stairs at all. The question was general but he answered with respect to the stairs only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Bourgon, but we would prefer if you are more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'll move on, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And ask him what he agrees with and what he doesn't agree with.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Will do, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'd like to move on, Mr. Tanic, to an issue concerning your military knowledge. We've heard during your examination-in-chief that you were the treasurer of the brigade and what you did since the beginning. But a couple of questions concerning your knowledge and I refer here to your interview, and that is on page 86921, for reference to my colleague, where you said, "I had no knowledge of the Zvornik Brigade involvement in combat operations." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: In what sense, you mean? What is the context? I didn't take part in combat operations. That is what it -- what may be said. I don't know about anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But did you have any knowledge of the combat operations? Because in that interview, you said you had no knowledge of combat operations.

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: I don't know when, what, how. I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let me quote the exact sentence in your interview, where it says, now, again, this is page 86921 and it says, "I was not related to operational activities so I have no specific knowledge about that issue." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I have no answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I move on to again your interview on page 86926, where you mention that you were not too familiar with the military structure. Would that be accurate?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I was in the medical corps in the army, and it didn't really interest me but during the war either, I wasn't interested in the specifics of it, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I move on to in your testimony, and I quote from page 12020, lines 2 to 4, where you stated, concerning Drago Nikolic, "We called him security officer in the brigade, but establishment-wise, I don't know his exact position." Do you stand by this statement today?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: I don't know in what sense. I know that the security organ exists and he was head of -- I don't know how to put it. I think that is what I stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That's exactly what I'm saying. You stated that you did not know so I'm just asking you to confirm, simply yes or no, unless you want to provide information.

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Only chief of security in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I move on to the issue of the day that you were invited to go to Orahovac and that you were in Standard and I'd just like to you confirm that on that day, when you went into that truck, that there were other soldiers in that truck. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you did not know who these soldiers were; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: I knew all of them but I can't recollect their names. They knew me and I know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you mentioned in your interview that this was the shift from Jelacici. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: That's what I heard, yes, that's what I heard. It doesn't mean that I know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you also mentioned that these people were kind of picked up by chance at the end of their shift and then they ended up just like you in Orahovac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: They were at Standard and they ended up in Orahovac. They were heading for the barracks. Anyway it was with them that I reached Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would I be right in saying that you cannot tell even today whether these soldiers were from the Zvornik Brigade or from another brigade?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Those in the truck were from the Zvornik Brigade, those who were with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I now move on to the next section, which is that of your knowledge at the time you were asked to go to Orahovac. Now, it is my understanding that this, when you were asked, someone told you that people were trying to escape; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, as to the time in your interview, on page 86936, you mention that for sure it was not morning but you could not confirm as suggested by the investigator that this took place between noon and 2.00 in the afternoon. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: I don't know that someone suggested it but it was in the afternoon probably. It wasn't in the morning but around noon, that's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I'd just like to come back to page 11998 of your testimony at line 20. And on that occasion, the question was: Do you know what unit these men belong to? If you don't know them personally?" And your answer was, at lines 19 and 20, "I don't know but I think it was the shift from Jelacici. I don't know if it can be established now what that group was." Do you stand by this statement today?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: I don't know what to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, do you agree with what you said then or --

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: It's not clear to me. I've said once already. A moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, when you were asked to go to Orahovac, would I be right in saying that no one ever mentioned the possibility that there would be some shooting down there? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: They only said that people were escaping and we needed to go there but before that I think people from the logistics went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And it's my understanding from your testimony today as well as from your prior testimony that somehow you knew that prisoners were in that school but you had no knowledge what would happen to them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: I didn't know, because the bus I mentioned, the more one says, one has more problems. The bus that was in the compound, it went around the facilities looking for room to house them. Now, I can't give you a precise answer to your question, yes, they were in schools, it was noon, et cetera. There was such a story. But when I was told that the prisoners were escaping that means that they were there. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So would I be right in saying following from your answer that you just gave, that the knowledge you had about prisoners being detained in the school was your own conclusion because they told you that prisoners were escaping? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: No. Even before that, there was some information, but I can't claim with 100 per cent certainty that there was some particular statement. I didn't make my own conclusion. But I assume so. I can't be exclusive. I can't say specifically yes, that's how it was. So I'm not specific in confirming what you have just said. I cannot do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. I now move to the time when you are in Orahovac, and what I'd like to establish with you is the sequence of events as they took place for you in Orahovac. Now, would I be right in saying that the first thing that happened is that the vehicle dropped you close to the fence near the gym? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that during the time that you left the vehicle, that you remained on the road along with Cedo Jovic?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that as soon as you had an opportunity, you went where you say those stairs were because you wanted to get away from there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. It's not like that. You're asking me to give you the chronology. I can't do that in that way. It's a fact that I was there with Cedo. I was on the road. That's what I stated, that I moved up and down and that I entered the yard and saw what I saw as I stated it. So I can't give you a precise chronology, minute by minute, because my recollections also vary, they jump from one period of time to another. I can't tell you with precision stage by stage. I just can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I'm not looking for a precise timing of what you did but I'm just trying to establish so that the Trial Chamber is clear as to your -- how much time you spent close to the gym. So would I be right in saying that you did not spend much time earlier on and then you went where those stairs were? Do you recall going towards those stairs?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. But then after those stairs, and from the forester's house, I would come back to see whether anyone was looking for me, whether there were any problems for me. I just didn't get away before seeing whether I was able to do what I wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when you went close to these stairs, would I be right in saying that at that time you were with Milan Savic and Mihajlo Stevanovic?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that shortly thereafter, you went across the street and you had coffee with these guys in a house that was close by?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: It's not a street. It's an area between the stairs and the next house. It was behind the cultural centre but there wasn't a street there, a road. I didn't cross the street. It is behind the building, both the house and the stairs are behind the cultural centre and behind the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We will have a chance to look at a plan of Orahovac later on but my next question is that you did go there and have coffee with those two individuals, Stevanovic and Savic?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And after a short while, you then left and you went to the house of Mira Vidovic where you stayed until 11.00 at night?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Yes, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You mentioned today in your testimony 8.00 but I quote here from your interview at page 86934, where you say that you stayed at her place, meaning Mira Vidovic, until 11.00. Which one would be more accurate? Would it be correct to say that it was around 11.00 that you left her house?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't count. You mean when I left her house? Possibly 11.00. It could have been 11.00. I didn't look at the time. I didn't mean that precisely. I didn't have a watch.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And while you were at the house of Mira Vidovic, you drank five or six brandies or rakija; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. They were small, you know, really small. I'm saying that sincerely, over the seven or eight hours that I spent there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when you decided to leave her place, you had decided to walk back to Zvornik Brigade headquarters or the command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And it's my understanding that you were accustomed to walking distances like that, that is something that you did regularly; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, the exact place where that vehicle picked you up that night, I believe you mention it today in your testimony but now I quote from both the -- from the interview at page 86934, saying that you walked about 100 to 150 metres and that's where that truck picked you up. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Something like that. The house is still standing there and I didn't measure it, but that's roughly the distance. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, this house of Mira Vidovic, can you confirm that this house is close to the main road, that is the second house from the restaurant Dolina Mira and that's -- can you confirm what kind of distance is it from the Orahovac school?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: More than one kilometre. I think some people from the Defence teams measured it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So it would be anywhere between 1 and 2 kilometres or at least 1 kilometre? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: A kilometre and a half, if you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, at that point in time you testified today that when you got out of the house you put five bullets in the frame of your M-48 rifle. Can you provide more information as to what led you to put at that time bullets in your rifle?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: A clip. It was a clip. It was night. And it was not very safe, I thought. I just wanted to have it, and I put it directly in the rifle because the munitions scattered.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that's when the rifle blocked, as you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: A piece of paper got stuck in the housing in the bearing. I saw that in the morning and I wasn't able to pull the safety lock. I tried to put in the ammunition and I wasn't able to pull the safety lock back. That piece of paper got stuck inside and I couldn't remove it. The person in charge of the weapons did it for me the next day, and that's the first time I realised the piece of paper had gotten stuck in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So I conclude from what you're saying that your weapon was not fired at all that day and that it was repaired the next morning; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: I did not. I did not fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to quote here from page 86948 of your interview, where you mention, and I will quote here the exact line, I do not have lines on this page but I will quote it directly: "So I tried to stay as little as possible near the school so I just got there, I saw what I saw, I had this conversation with the people there, the staircase, a few comments were made, and then I went to my friend's house." Is that a good recollection of what you did in Orahovac that afternoon and that night?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Well, I've already described how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But what I just read, does that correspond? Because those are your words from your interview.

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Well, maybe this is the abbreviated version, but...

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I quote now also from what you mentioned today, and that was on page 35 at lines 11 to 16, and you said something very similar in your interview, at page 86960, and would I be right in saying that you saw one truck being loaded and that's when you walked away towards the staircase?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: It's difficult to put a time-line on it now. I wasn't following anymore what was going on outside the gym. I just saw, when the first people started getting onto the truck, and then I stopped paying attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: At lines 11 to 16, you mention, and I quote from lines 12, "Well, I was there until the first group started boarding a truck. I did not wait for them to finish boarding the truck. When the first group started boarding the truck, I could already see." So would I be right in saying that you saw the first truck being loaded and then you did not stay there and you didn't wait for them to finish and you left towards the staircase?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: It's not questionable where I went. I just stopped watching at some point. I just saw the first people boarding the truck. You're asking too much after all these years. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I fully realise that it's not easy to remember everything that you might have seen. But we'll give it a try any way. The -- I'd like to quote now from page 86987 from your interview. And you stated at that time that you stayed -- okay, here I have it. This was a question that was put to you. Okay, how much time approximately did you spend in front of the school? Or in close vicinity of the school? And your answer was, "So you know from the afternoon, maybe two hours, then I went to Mira Vidovic's place." Is that a good recollection of the events?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Two or three hours. You're really asking too much. I'm really not able to tell you with such precision. I don't even know exactly when I came to Mira's house. I cannot tell you three hours, 15 minutes, or four hours. I have no idea. I can only say roughly that I was there for two or three hours, around the school, and then I left. All this is roughly speaking. I'm not trying to -- I don't mean that very precisely. I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I understand. I fully understand, Witness, Mr. Tanic. I'm just going over your interview because those are things that you stated at one time, maybe you don't recall today, but at one time you stated two hours. So would I be right in saying is it closer to two hours or closer to four hours, for example?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: How am I supposed to know that? I didn't even know it precisely back then, let alone now. You really are asking too much. People are asking me nowadays whether I made a mistake then or I made a mistake today, or I made a mistake in between or whether it was a mistake coming here at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would I be right in saying that from the time that you reach Mira Vidovic's place, until the time you left her house at 11.00 at night or thereabouts, you have no knowledge of anything that happened near the school in Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Let's say I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to move, for the time we have left, with some of the things that you -- that you may have seen or failed to see in Orahovac, always quoting from your interview, just to see if you can confirm. And I'd like to start with page 86932 where you mention that you were not familiar with Orahovac before the events that day. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Not much. Maybe I passed by a couple of times before, maybe I was there once in 1993 but I don't really know the layout of the houses and...

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Tanic, what did you understand your task to be when you arrive in Orahovac? What were you there for?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: I believe everybody from the logistics was rounded up and sent there. My understanding was that prisoners were running away and I believed that, I thought to myself, well, that's possible, and I was needed to help out. That's how I understood that invitation. I think I answered this question before. Now if I say two or three words differently you'll pin me down on it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The aim, Mr. Tanic, is not to pin you down but simply to recall what you mentioned earlier and then to obtain from you -- either you can correct it or you can just say that generally the information is correct. Now, I quote now from page 86945 of your interview. Today in your testimony you saw -- you mention seeing boys carrying water. Would I be right in saying that these boys were accompanied by a soldier?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, on that page, at 86945, you mentioned that you could not tell whether these soldiers were from the Zvornik Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: I don't remember saying that. I don't understand the drift of your question. Which soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go back. You testified today that you saw two boys carrying water and that they were accompanied by a soldier. And you mention on that occasion that you could not tell whether these soldiers were from Zvornik Brigade. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think my colleague is referring to 86945 of the interview; is that correct? I don't see that there is a reference to the specific soldiers in the plural. There is, I believe, a reference to the particular soldier that the witness was talking about and I think the question should be framed in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I thank my colleague for this. It's one soldier and not many soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So Mr. Tanic, it was one soldier and I will quote your exact word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The question which was asked of you was, did you recognise that soldier? And your answer was no. The next question was: "He was a Zvornik Brigade soldier?" Your answer was, "I cannot say. I cannot tell exactly because, you know, I know a lot of people and there were a lot of people there so I cannot tell who it was from which brigade, saw so many faces." Do you stand by this -- by your answer?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: I don't see the point of this question. What am I supposed to say now? When did I say that? Did I say that today? I lost track already.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: This was mentioned during your interview with the Prosecution in 2002. So that's five years ago. So --

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Well, you should say that straight away. I thought it's something I said today. I can still remember what I said today; since 2002 I have already forgotten certain things.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, of course, it's a very likely to -- very normal to forget some things that go back to 2002 but in terms of the exact words that you used. Now, at that time, you mentioned that you did not recognise this soldier and you did not know whether he was from Zvornik Brigade. What could you say today? Do you recall? Could you identify this soldier or still you could not identify him and you don't know if he is from the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: I don't know but I think I said that before to the Prosecution and to you. It's a soldier, right? Therefore, if I told that to you, then I said the same to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, this answer was given to the Prosecution during the interview in 2002. I'm just asking if you could confirm --

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, recently, I mean. Not in 2002. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The text I quoted from, Mr. Tanic, is from 2002. Now I'm simply asking you today, regardless of that text because I was using a reference for the sake of allowing my colleague where I was going with my question but I'm just asking you now do you recall if you recognised that soldier and whether you still cannot tell he was -- whether he was from Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: I said that to the Prosecution as well. It was a soldier from the Zvornik Brigade, and I think I told you the same things but I didn't think that you would be asking me this because you said you wouldn't. Now, you are starting to ask me things that -- all right? All right. But that's what the story was before. You can use it but then you are abusing my confidence. Okay, okay, we can move on. I told you and the Prosecution the same thing, in our last conversation. I didn't lie for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So what you're saying today, Mr. Tanic, is that he was from the Zvornik Brigade? That's all I'm asking you, whether he was or wasn't.

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I quote again from your interview, that is 2002, with the Prosecution, they asked you whether the truck was covered and your answer was that -- I'm talking about the truck that you saw beginning to be loaded. And your response was, "I know the truck was covered but I cannot specify the make or the type." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And on page 86948, you mention that --

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: I don't know. You are going into too much detail for me. I told them even then, I can't remember the wheels, the tarpaulin. You can ask, of course, but I really don't see the point. I said it was a small truck that it had a tarpaulin cover, whether it was yellow, blue or orange.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tanic, the purpose of my question is simply to confirm what you said earlier, nothing more, nothing less, and I was exactly --

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: What I said earlier is what I meant. I said it was a small truck. There was a tarpaulin truck. Maybe I was wrong about the colour. So what? Am I responsible, guilty, for getting the colour wrong?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Not at all, Mr. Tanic. The -- let me simply mention to you for the sake of clarification that the text I'm quoting from is not available to the Judges. That's why I simply want to you confirm what is in that text in certain places in that text; you understand that?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: All right, then. Okay. Ask, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you mention about the truck. Now I just come back, you already confirmed today, just a few minutes ago, that you did not see the colour of the truck. Now, would I be right in saying or what you said that you could -- you did not identify the driver of the truck; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know who drove the truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, there was one thing that I will quote from page 86949 of the interview of 2002, something that you mention, and you stated, I will quote the exact words, "I found out later --" well, let me ask the question so that we are -- for the sake of completeness. The question was, "You knew people were being shot in that school, didn't you?" And your answer was, "I found out later." So later, they, they were put on trucks and taken away. And we could hear shots." So that's later that you find this out; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand a word you said. I would need to read the full statement and review it again. Right now, hearing it like this, taken out of the context, I really don't follow what you're asking me at all. I'm very sorry but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can stop here for today, because I see signs of tiredness. We continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, in order to assist the witness tomorrow I have on the e-court the statement in his language so he can also read it and that will be -- I guess, it would be easier for him because I just want to confirm certain aspects of his statement. Thank you very much, Mr. Tanic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are authorising the handing to the witness of his statement so that we can continue tomorrow. Witness, Mr. Tanic, we will continue tomorrow in the afternoon, which allows you time to rest after this morning's testimony. Tomorrow, I'm confident that we will finish with your testimony and that you will be free to go back home at the earliest. In the meantime between today and tomorrow, until you finish your testimony you are not to contact or allow anyone to contact you to discuss or speak about the matters of your testimony. Is that clear enough? You're not allowed to approach anyone or allow anyone to approach you to discuss these matters. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean nobody, even the people here? You mean when I go outside I'm not supposed to talk to anybody or I'm not supposed to talk to the lawyers here in the courtroom or what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope that on the way out, you will not come across any of the lawyers, Prosecution or Defence. You are not to speak or to contact anyone on the matters which you are testifying upon, and that includes everyone. All right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Very well. And I'm not supposed to have coffee with anyone either? You mean I'm not supposed to talk at all? I don't understand. Suppose I want to go and have a coffee with one of the people here I know? I cannot, for instance, go and have a cup with -- I mean, without talking about the case? No way. I'm very sorry if I didn't get this right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It will be -- it will make us very angry if we come to know that you even tried to have a coffee with anyone who is in this courtroom at the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now it's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But of course you can have a coffee with anyone else provided that you do not touch upon or you do not allow the other person to touch upon the matters that you're testifying upon. I hope that is clear now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. So we'll meet tomorrow afternoon at quarter past 2.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
